newsitem.title: CUBA: Castro to celebrate 71, more taciturn than usual.
newsitem.headline: Castro to celebrate 71, more taciturn than usual.

text.p: Cuba's President Fidel Castro turns 71 on Wednesday, but after 38 years in power the defiant guardian of communism is in less vocal form than usual.
Castro has not made a public speech since early April and at some recent public appearances he has looked tired, leading to speculation in some quarters that he may be ill.

State television on Saturday showed him speaking with a group of Cuban journalists, lamenting the "disaster" of the collapse of communism in the former Soviet bloc. The Cuban leader looked in normal health.
Castro, one of the world's longest-serving leaders,is well known for his long public speeches, but he has periodically lapsed into silence in the past.
"It's true he hasn't made a public speech for a while, but he has done this in the past, and he may be saving himself for the (Communist) Party Congress," said one Western diplomat.
The October 8-10 party congress, the first since 1991, is this year's major political event and will set Cuba's national economic and political strategy into the next century.

A party document issued for national debate ahead of the congress makes plain the leadership intends to stick with the one-party communist system, even if Cuba has been forced into cautious economic liberalisation over the past four years.

Castro, in power since the 1959 revolution that toppled former dictator Fulgencio Batista, attended the opening and closing ceremonies of a July 28-Aug 5 international leftist youth festival, but he did not speak on either occasion.
The Cuban leader also presided over but did not speak at ceremonies to mark July 26 -- the anniversary of the launch of his guerrilla struggle in 1953 and a key date in Cuba's revolutionary calendar.

Castro gave the task of that speech to his younger brother Raul Castro, who is deputy president, defence minister and Fidel Castro's designated successor should the Cuban leader die or become incapacitated.

Raul Castro's address included a reiteration of Cuba's charge that people from the United States are behind a recent spate of small bombings aimed at Cuba's tourism industry -- an accusation Washington has demanded Cuba substantiate.

Two bombs went off on July 12 in the lobbies of the Nacional and Capri hotels in Havana, causing some damage and slightly injuring three people. Another small bomb exploded on Aug 4. at Havana's Melia Cohiba hotel, damaging the lobby. The previous day, a bomb damaged the office of a Cuban state tourism firm, Havanatur, in Nassau in the Bahamas.

Castro's birthday celebrations are likely to be low key. Official discretion over the Cuban leader's private life has traditionally extended to his birthdays and it is unlikely Castro will make any special appearance.
On Sunday, the youth communist newspaper Juventud Rebelde published a tribute headlined "Congratulations, COMMANDER".

Last year, as he turned 70, there was more fanfare. State media published several homages. Castro was invited to a party by the Young Pioneers, Cuba's communist youth organisation, where he beamingly cut a birthday cake.
Unusually, Castro mused then on his feelings about life.
"I'm aware I'm not immortal, or anything like it. I am flesh and blood, but that doesn't startle me or worry me," he said, adding that Cuba's political system should survive him.
"This is a revolution that has been made, nobody can undo it," he said.
